name: T05-ai-coding-tool

adversarial_competitor.summary: How I would kill this: ship a free "Beginner Mode — simple explanations" toggle inside our existing coding assistant and publish dozens of SEO-first "error → plain-English fix" pages to own discovery — because that duplicates the product's only claimed differentiation and we can match or beat pricing and distribution with near-zero incremental cost. Survive it by: locking exclusive distribution with bootcamps/IDEs or embedding into an IDE by default so users can't discover or trial the feature elsewhere. With our engineering and content teams this is a two-week front-end + prompt engineering task and a one-month SEO/content push; we then bury their positioning behind our brand, app-store placement, and freemium funnel.

flaws.title: Single-claim defensibility: "simpler explanations" is not a moat
flaws.description: The founder's only stated differentiation is simpler explanations, which is trivially replicable by incumbents via a UI toggle, prompt templates, or a curated content feed. There is no proprietary model, dataset, pedagogy, or exclusive distribution that prevents others from matching the same output quality. If an incumbent ships a beginner toggle or adds a curated errors FAQ, the product's unique claim becomes meaningless and user acquisition collapses.
flaws.question: What proprietary, hard-to-copy asset (data, partnership, credential, or integration) makes your "simpler explanations" defensible against incumbents who can ship the same feature quickly?

flaws.title: Price is irrelevant without distribution — incumbents can undercut or bundle
flaws.description: Charging 12 per month is only meaningful if you reach users cheaply and prevent commoditization. Well-funded competitors can add a free beginner tier, bundle this feature into existing subscriptions, or give it away to acquire users, making a stand-alone 12/month offer uncompetitive. The founder gives no plan for resisting pricing pressure from products that already amortize customer acquisition across many features.
flaws.question: Why will beginners pay 12 per month when incumbents can offer the same feature free or bundled into an existing plan?

flaws.title: No go-to-market; distribution advantages squarely favor incumbents
flaws.description: The document contains no acquisition strategy. Incumbents control the high-leverage channels for code-help discovery (IDE integrations, app stores, plugin marketplaces, large existing user bases, and SEO). With our distribution we can push the same feature via an update, email, app-store placement, and organic search to millions instantly, blocking the founder's ability to gain traction.
flaws.question: Which specific channels will you use to scale acquisition cheaply and how will you capture discovery that IDEs, search and app stores already own?

flaws.title: No evidence users will pay instead of using free docs/Stack Overflow
flaws.description: Beginners already use free resources (official docs, Q&A, tutorials). The founder provides no demand evidence that beginners will pay 12 per month for simpler explanations rather than continuing to use free sources. The cheapest way to test this is a low-cost landing page or $1 pilot to measure purchase intent before building.
flaws.question: Can you demonstrate willingness-to-pay from your target beginners with a landing-page pre-sale, $1 pilot, or validated sign-up funnel?

flaws.title: Target buyer is too vague; 'beginner programmers' is a heterogeneous market
flaws.description: Beginners include bootcamp students, CS majors, hobbyists, and career-changers; their needs and willingness to pay vary widely. The plan doesn't specify which segment to prioritize first or how the product will adapt explanations for different learning contexts. Without a focused initial buyer, acquisition messaging and product requirements will be inconsistent and easy for incumbents to out-execute.
flaws.question: Which exact beginner segment are you targeting first (e.g., bootcamp students, hobbyists, CS1 students) and why will that segment pay 12 per month?

unit_economics.summary: Where the math breaks: cost-to-serve per user — because you list a $12/month price but provide no itemized per-user costs (compute, storage, support, payment fees) so revenue and margin are pure hope. Prove otherwise by: supplying an itemized per-user cost estimate measured from a small pilot (for example, 1,000 sessions — assuming you can run that pilot) showing average compute tokens, model cost, storage, support time, and payment fees. Without those figures you cannot know if $12 covers variable costs, whether CAC can be paid back, or whether the business reaches positive gross margin at scale; the rest of the unit-economics questions (CAC, LTV, payback) depend on that baseline.

flaws.title: No per-user cost estimate (compute, storage, support, payments)
flaws.description: You state a $12/month price but give zero breakdown of the variable costs that determine gross margin. For an AI coding assistant the dominant line item is model inference (tokens × model price), which can swamp a $12 price if not measured and optimized. Without an itemized per-user cost you cannot tell whether the product is profitable at any scale.
flaws.question: What is your measured per-user cost broken down by compute (average tokens per session × model price), storage, support time, and payment processing fees?

flaws.title: Willingness-to-pay for $12/month is unvalidated
flaws.description: You picked $12/month but provide no evidence that beginner programmers will pay that amount for simpler explanations. Free alternatives and integrated IDE tools are common; pricing must be supported by conversion or willingness-to-pay data. If customers won't pay $12, CAC and payback calculations are moot.
flaws.question: What evidence (paid pilot conversions, pricing tests, or survey-to-purchase data) shows beginners will pay $12/month rather than use free competitors?

flaws.title: No acquisition plan or CAC estimates
flaws.description: Your strategy lacks any acquisition channels or CAC estimates; at $12/mo CAC must be low or payback impossible. Channels that scale (ads, partnerships, content) have measurable costs and conversion rates — none are provided, so the claim of viable unit economics is unsupported. Viral or organic growth is asserted implicitly but not shown.
flaws.question: Which acquisition channels will you use, what is the expected CAC per paid user for each, and how do you expect to achieve that CAC at a $12 price point?

flaws.title: No gross-margin model or forward scaling assumptions
flaws.description: You do not present a current gross-margin estimate or how margins improve (or worsen) as you scale. LLM inference costs, caching, and support overhead can change materially with scale; without a pro forma you cannot judge whether margins converge to acceptable levels. This prevents assessment of unit economics at target scale.
flaws.question: Provide a unit-economics pro forma showing gross margin per user today and projected at a scale milestone (e.g., 10k or 100k paying users) with assumptions made explicit.

flaws.title: No LTV / CAC / payback calculation
flaws.description: You give price but no LTV (average months of retention × ARPU) and no CAC, so payback period is unknown. Without LTV/CAC you cannot determine if acquisition spend is justified or what lifetime revenue supports initial marketing investment. Payback period determines runway needs and growth cadence, but it's not computed.
flaws.question: What is your expected LTV (average lifetime in months × 12×$12 or ARPU) and how many months to recover CAC at your assumed CAC?

flaws.title: Operational/hidden costs (moderation, refunds, fraud) are unaccounted
flaws.description: You do not mention moderation, developer support, compliance, refunds/chargebacks, or fraud prevention — all can add significant per-user costs. Code advice can create liability or support load (e.g., debugging sessions), and payment refunds/chargebacks are common for subscription products. These hidden costs will reduce gross margin and can break payback assumptions.
flaws.question: How will you quantify and budget for moderation, developer support time, refunds/chargebacks, and fraud prevention per user?

pre_mortem.summary: Most likely killer: pricing/demand mismatch — because the plan fixes a $12/month subscription for beginner programmers without any evidence that beginners will pay for 'simpler explanations'. Prove otherwise by: running a payment-commitment landing-page test at $12/month (real payment or card hold) and measuring whether target beginners convert at a rate that would justify continuing. Supporting synthesis: The idea rests on three untested assumptions at once — that beginners will pay a subscription, that an AI can reliably produce simpler and correct explanations, and that those explanations are worth switching away from free workflows. Any one of those failing stops this strategy; pricing is the most immediate gatekeeper because payment converts stated interest into revealed demand quickly and cheaply.

flaws.title: Pricing set without evidence — target users won't commit to $12/mo
flaws.description: Failure scenario: the founder charges $12/month but target beginners sign up at negligibly low rates because they prefer free resources or one-off help. The document gives a price but no evidence that beginners are willing to pay a recurring subscription for explanations. If buyers won't commit to the price, the product never reaches traction regardless of feature quality.
flaws.question: Will a representative sample of target beginner programmers commit payment when asked to subscribe at $12/month on a live landing page?

flaws.title: AI cannot reliably produce consistently simple, correct fixes for beginners
flaws.description: Failure scenario: the assistant's explanations are either too technical, inconsistent in tone, or occasionally incorrect, and beginners cannot distinguish wrong guidance from right guidance. The plan assumes the AI can translate diverse error messages into concise, actionable, beginner-friendly steps, but the document gives no evidence or requirement about accuracy thresholds or guardrails. If explanations mislead learners, trust and retention will collapse even if initial interest exists.
flaws.question: Can the system produce concise, correct, beginner-level explanations and fixes across a representative set of common beginner errors with an acceptably low error/harm rate in a blind evaluation?

flaws.title: Stated preference likely differs from revealed preference
flaws.description: Failure scenario: beginners say they want 'simpler explanations' in surveys but when faced with the actual decision choose free search, forum answers, or video tutorials over a paid subscription. The document assumes verbal demand implies willingness to pay and to change existing habits, but no demand evidence or prototype testing is provided. If revealed preferences favor existing free workflows, conversion will be too low to sustain a subscription model.
flaws.question: When given the real choice between continuing with free search/community resources and paying for instant simpler explanations, which do target beginners pick?

flaws.title: No plan for how to reach beginner payers
flaws.description: Failure scenario: even if some beginners would pay, the team cannot find a repeatable, scalable acquisition channel and so only attracts non-paying users or a tiny niche. The document states who the product is for but says nothing about acquisition channels, distribution partnerships, or integrations (IDE/plugin, bootcamps, schools). Without a tested channel to get paying customers, the product can't scale from idea to revenue.
flaws.question: What single, testable channel will deliver paying beginner users at an efficient and repeatable rate?

flaws.title: Differentiation — 'simpler explanations' is vague and may not beat free alternatives
flaws.description: Failure scenario: 'simpler explanations' turns out to be insufficiently specific or reproducible to persuade users to switch from free tools that already give explanations (docs, search, community). The document claims differentiation but provides no specifics on format, integration, response time, or measurable benefits that would make the product clearly superior. If differentiation cannot be articulated and demonstrated, users have little reason to pay.
flaws.question: What exact capability or output (format, turnaround, integration) will make a beginner choose this product over free documentation, search, and community answers?

execution_risk.summary: What breaks first: user acquisition — because you priced a consumer product at 12 per month and promised to 'compete' with existing AI coding tools, but you have no channel or evidence that beginner programmers will discover or pay for this instead of free alternatives. Prevent it by: validating demand and willingness-to-pay immediately with a landing page, pre-orders or credit-card gated trials and a small paid acquisition test before building the product. If that test fails, don't build integrations; rework target, value prop, or pricing. Beyond acquisition, the core technical correctness of suggested fixes and data-handling rules are not addressed and will block adoption even if you drive traffic.

flaws.title: No acquisition plan — build it and no one shows up
flaws.description: The document gives a price and a positioning claim but contains zero channel, funnel, or conversion plan. Concrete failure mode: the team spends months building an MVP and integrations only to find organic traffic is nil and paid conversion to 12 per month is far below break-even, leaving the product without users. This will consume runway and prevent any real learning about demand.
flaws.question: How will you acquire your first cohort of paying beginner programmers and prove conversion at 12 per month before you build integrations?

flaws.title: Price set without evidence against free alternatives
flaws.description: Founder explicitly set 12 per month but provided no evidence that beginners will pay that rather than use free LLM chat, free student offers, or built-in IDE help. Concrete failure mode: conversion rates to a paid plan are near-zero because the perceived incremental value over free tools is insufficient, so subscriptions never scale. This pricing assertion is a stated fact with no validation.
flaws.question: What evidence do you have that beginners will pay 12 per month for simpler explanations rather than using free alternatives?

flaws.title: Core product risk: suggested fixes will be wrong or harmful
flaws.description: The entire value proposition depends on reliably explaining errors and recommending correct fixes for novices; the doc has no plan to measure or ensure fix accuracy. Concrete failure mode: the assistant suggests incorrect fixes that teach bad habits or break users' code, causing churn, bad reviews, and potential safety/legal complaints from educators or employers. Without an accuracy threshold and a mitigation plan, you cannot charge or scale.
flaws.question: How will you measure and guarantee the accuracy and safety of suggested fixes for beginners before taking money?

flaws.title: Sequencing mistake: integrations before core validation
flaws.description: No minimum viable product or sequencing is defined; building VS Code/IDE plugins, authentication, and billing before validating the core explanatory model will waste time. Concrete failure mode: months spent on plugins and infrastructure lock you into product assumptions while the core model doesn't meet user needs. The cheapest test would be a web-based copy-paste flow or a demo bot to validate explanations first.
flaws.question: What is your minimum testable product and why will you delay editor integrations until you validate core demand and model quality?

flaws.title: Data handling and compliance are unspecified
flaws.description: You will be processing users' code, which can contain PII or proprietary IP, but there's no plan for storage, retention, consent, or third-party model provider TOS compliance. Concrete failure mode: schools, employers, or platform providers refuse to allow the product, or you face takedown/contract issues from model vendors, blocking distribution to meaningful channels. Early adopters will not attach sensitive code without clear guarantees.
flaws.question: How will you store/process user code, what retention/consent controls will you implement, and how will you meet privacy and provider-TOS requirements?

flaws.title: Team and timeline not stated — scope underestimated
flaws.description: No team, roles, or timeline are listed; building reliable explanations, model tuning, integrations, analytics, and support is multi-disciplinary work. Concrete failure mode: a single founder or tiny team splits attention across model, product, and marketing, leading to slow delivery and poor product quality. This underestimation will extend ship time well beyond expectations.
flaws.question: Who will build and maintain the model, product, integrations, and customer support, and what is the realistic timeline to an MVP?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Weak. Weakest number: the claim that beginners will pay $12/month for 'simpler explanations' — because there is no willingness-to-pay or paid-conversion evidence. Prove it by running a paid pilot or priced landing page and report unique visitors, paid signups (≥20), and conversion rate. Currently nothing is proven: no validated demand, price, CAC, comparative preference, or correctness benchmarks.

flaws.title: No evidence beginners will buy simpler explanations
flaws.description: The core claim is that beginner programmers will prefer and pay for 'simpler explanations', but there is no measured demand evidence (no survey, no landing page, no paid pilot). If beginners do not value simplicity over free/established tools, revenue never materializes. This is the load-bearing customer demand gap for the whole plan.
flaws.question: Provide empirical demand evidence: run a landing page or paid pilot targeting beginner programmers and report the number of unique visitors (N), number who signed up for a paid $12/month trial, and the resulting paid-conversion rate (report raw counts).

flaws.title: Price ($12/month) is unsupported and untested
flaws.description: The only revenue figure given is $12 per month; there is no willingness-to-pay data or conversion metrics. Annualized revenue per paying user is $12 × 12 = $144 per year, but that number is meaningless without showing users will actually pay. If $12 is above what beginners will accept, unit economics collapse.
flaws.question: Show price-validation: either (a) results from a price-sensitivity survey or Van Westendorp test, or (b) a paid pilot reporting at least 20 paid conversions at $12/month (report counts and conversion rate).

flaws.title: No acquisition evidence or CAC estimate
flaws.description: The strategy lacks any plan or measured data for how you will reach beginner programmers or what it costs. Without a measured CAC, you cannot test whether acquisition cost is below customer lifetime value (which depends on the unvalidated $12 price). If CAC exceeds what a $12/month customer can support, the business is unviable.
flaws.question: Provide measured acquisition test results: for at least one channel, report spend, unique users reached, signups and paid conversions so I can compute CAC (spend ÷ paid customers) from actual experiments.

flaws.title: No evidence you can outcompete established tools on 'simpler explanations'
flaws.description: You assert differentiation via simpler explanations but provide no comparative evidence versus existing AI tools (e.g., readability, comprehension, successful fixes). If customers prefer diagnostic accuracy, speed, or editor integration over simplicity, the differentiator fails. The claim needs head-to-head measurement.
flaws.question: Provide a comparative user test: present the same error to N beginner programmers with answers from an existing tool and your explanation, and report preference and comprehension metrics (N, preference counts, and time-to-fix).

flaws.title: No examples or technical proof that the assistant can reliably produce simpler, correct fixes
flaws.description: There are no sample outputs, benchmarks or correctness rates showing the assistant can both simplify explanations and suggest correct fixes. Simpler wording that is incorrect or misleading will harm adoption; you need samples and small-scale labeling to confirm quality.
flaws.question: Provide 50 real beginner error instances and your assistant's proposed explanations/fixes for each, plus an expert or user-rated correctness/clarity score (report raw counts and average scores).

Prove otherwise by selling real paid access at $12 to target beginner users (preorders or paid trials) before building the product. The founder has no customer interviews, no acquisition plan, and a vague value proposition; the likeliest failure is that stated desire for simpler explanations will not become revealed willingness-to-pay.

If the actual payer is institutions or teachers, the product, pricing and go-to-market must be different. Without naming and testing the payer, the project can be built for a user who will never convert to revenue.
flaws.question: Who exactly will pay $12/month for this product (individual beginners, parents, schools, employers), and what evidence shows that group will pay?

flaws.title: No evidence beginners will pay (stated vs revealed preference)
flaws.description: The founder admits they haven't asked any beginner programmers and relies on personal learning experience. Beginners often state they want help but prefer free channels in practice; assuming they will subscribe is a direct leap from stated preference to revenue. If willingness-to-pay is absent, acquisition and retention cannot produce subscriptions.
flaws.question: Can you get paid commitments from multiple representative beginner programmers at $12/month before you build the product?

flaws.title: Price ($12/month) is arbitrary and unsupported
flaws.description: The document fixes a $12/month price with no justification, elasticity testing, or alternative pricing explored. That price might be above what beginners will pay for explanation-focused help or might require a different billing model (one-off, freemium, or institutional licensing). If the price point is wrong, conversions will fail even if the product is useful.
flaws.question: Why $12/month specifically, and what evidence shows target beginners prefer that pricing model over free, lower, or institutional pricing?

flaws.title: Differentiation 'simpler explanations' is vague and non-defensible
flaws.description: Claiming to compete by offering 'simpler explanations' is subjective and unscoped: simpler than what, measured how, for which errors, and for which languages/frameworks. If the feature cannot be operationalized into testable, repeatable outputs that demonstrably improve learning, users will not perceive enough unique value to switch or pay.
flaws.question: What exactly makes your explanations distinct and demonstrably better than existing free resources and how will you measure that difference?

flaws.title: No customer acquisition plan to reach paying beginners
flaws.description: There is no stated channel for finding and converting beginners into paying subscribers. Beginners are a broad group—some are students, others hobbyists—and their acquisition paths differ; without a tested channel and conversion mechanism the product cannot reach paying users. The absence of an acquisition hypothesis leaves the idea unable to scale even if demand exists.
flaws.question: Which specific channels will you use to acquire paying beginner users and what cheap experiment will you run to validate one channel works?

flaws.title: Current alternatives and switching costs are undocumented
flaws.description: The founder has not mapped what beginners use today when they encounter errors (docs, Stack Overflow, instructors, free AI assistants) nor how entrenched those behaviors are. Without this map you can't assess how hard it is to convince users to try a paid assistant or what features overcome switching friction.
flaws.question: What are the top three ways target beginners currently solve error/debugging problems, and why would they switch to your product?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Weak. Weakest number: $12/month price — because the founder explicitly admits they have not tested willingness-to-pay with beginner programmers. Prove it by a willingness-to-pay or landing-page pre-sell test among ≥100 beginners showing conversion to paid at $12. What is proven: only the idea and founder experience; no customer, pricing, or revenue evidence.

flaws.title: No evidence beginners will pay $12/month
flaws.description: The founder explicitly states they have not asked any beginner programmers whether they would pay; the $12/month price is therefore unsupported. Willingness-to-pay is load-bearing: if beginners will not pay, the product cannot earn revenue at the stated price. This is an idea-stage gap that must be resolved before any revenue projections or build decisions.
flaws.question: Provide results of a willingness-to-pay test among at least 100 beginner programmers (assuming 100 as a minimum sample): what % committed to a real or validated payment at $12/month?

flaws.title: No unit-economics: CAC, churn, LTV, payback are missing
flaws.description: Key load-bearing numbers (customer acquisition cost, expected churn, lifetime, and LTV) are not stated. Without these you cannot tell whether $12/month can cover acquisition and operating costs or what growth is viable. Any revenue or scaling claim is meaningless without at least empirically grounded or clearly sourced estimates for these metrics.
flaws.question: Provide projected or measured CAC, monthly churn, average revenue per user, and resulting LTV and payback period — and state the data source or experiment for each figure.

flaws.title: Paying buyer is underspecified beyond 'beginner programmers'
flaws.description: Saying the target is 'beginner programmers' does not identify who will actually pay (self-learners, students, bootcamps, parents, employers). Different buyers have different willingness-to-pay and acquisition paths; the plan depends on picking a paying segment and reaching them. This is an evidence gap not yet tested.
flaws.question: Define the specific paying buyer segment (e.g., self-taught beginners vs bootcamp students) and provide any evidence you have that this segment can be reached and will pay.

flaws.title: No evidence simpler explanations will beat existing tools
flaws.description: The competitive differentiator is 'simpler explanations' but there is no user testing showing beginners prefer simpler explanations over alternatives (accuracy, speed, integrated tooling). If simpler explanations do not improve perceived value, the product loses its USP. This is an assumption that must be validated with users.
flaws.question: Provide results of usability or preference tests showing beginners choose simpler explanations over alternatives (report metric, sample size, and test setup).

flaws.title: No acquisition or channel evidence — how will beginners find and try it?
flaws.description: The document gives no acquisition plan or any measured channel performance; without at least one validated channel and a conversion benchmark you cannot estimate scale or CAC. Acquisition assumptions drive required spend and feasibility of $12/month economics.
flaws.question: Show results from at least one acquisition test (e.g., landing page, ad, community post) with measured sign-up rate and cost per signup, or state the tested channel and measured conversion if available.

name: T06-video-economics

adversarial_competitor.summary: How I would kill this: Match the £5 "unlimited" plan immediately and subsidize it with our deeper pockets and distribution (free trials, onboarding credits, and prominent placement in app stores/SEO) — because their own numbers (≈£2 per generated video and 20 videos/month) make the product loss-leading and impossible to scale while we can out-spend and out-distribute them. Survive it by: publishing a clear fair-use policy and minimal throttles (or a small overage fee) so you can stop the bleeding and retain profitable users. Quick synthesis: we neutralize their headline differentiation (cheap unlimited) by offering the same promise briefly while leveraging existing users, app-store featuring, SEO, and partners to swamp their early traction; once they have no room to underprice us, we tighten usage controls or convert users to higher-margin plans.

flaws.title: Price + usage numbers guarantee unsustainable losses
flaws.description: You state a £5/month unlimited price, a per-video cost of approximately £2, and an expected 20 videos per subscriber. Those three claims cannot coexist: at your stated usage and cost you lose about £35 per subscriber per month before any overhead, so the plan is financially impossible to operate at scale. This is not a subtle optimization gap — it destroys the business model unless one of the three numbers changes immediately.
flaws.question: Which of these three is false or will change: the £5 price, the £2 per-video cost, or the 20 videos/month usage assumption?

flaws.title: ‘Unlimited’ video generation is not defensible technical differentiation
flaws.description: Generative video model access and cloud rendering are commodity capabilities to any well-funded competitor or cloud provider. Nothing in the plan claims proprietary models, exclusive data, or a lock-in that prevents incumbents from copying a similarly marketed unlimited tier. Without a clear moat, any small marketing push from an incumbent makes your offering redundant instantly.
flaws.question: What exclusive model IP, dataset, UX, or distribution lock prevents incumbents from replicating your 'unlimited' promise?

flaws.title: No customer acquisition plan — incumbents can drown you in distribution
flaws.description: You give a price and cost assumption but no acquisition channel, CPA target, or go-to-market. A competitor with a large user base, SEO authority, app-store relationships, and partner channel can promote a matching or better offer at near-zero incremental acquisition cost relative to your unknown plan. That advantage lets incumbents buy or give away early subscriptions to crush your growth runway.
flaws.question: How will you acquire customers at a cost that survives your stated unit economics, and what channels will you use to compete against incumbent distribution?

flaws.title: No evidence users will generate 20 videos or accept 5 per month pricing
flaws.description: You assume high usage (20 videos/month) and that customers will pay £5 for unlimited generation, but provide no demand tests, willingness-to-pay studies, or MVP learnings. If actual usage is lower or willingness-to-pay is lower/higher, pricing and capacity planning change dramatically. You need simple demand signals before building.
flaws.question: What experiments or survey data show users will both pay £5 and generate 20 videos per month?

flaws.title: Competition and substitutes are unspecified and easy to replicate
flaws.description: You do not list current alternatives—desktop editing, stock-video, short-form mobile apps, or existing AI tools—so you haven't shown why customers would switch. Incumbents with existing editing products can fold a priced plan into their UI faster than you can acquire meaningful share.
flaws.question: Which current products do your target customers use today for short-form video, and why will they switch to your service?

execution_risk.summary: What breaks first: unit economics — because at £5/month with ~£2 per video and an expected 20 videos per user you lose ~£35 per subscriber each month. Prevent it by: fix the unit economics before building anything (either raise price, add hard usage caps, or prove cost-per-video < £0.25) and show a reconciled per-subscriber P&L. The rest of the plan depends entirely on that fix: every technical, sequencing and distribution decision changes if price, cost or usage assumptions change.

flaws.title: Unit economics directly contradict the pricing model
flaws.description: You stated price = 5 and cost per video ≈ 2 with average 20 videos/month. That yields cost ≈ 40 per subscriber versus revenue 5, a negative 35 margin each month. This single numeric contradiction makes the stated business impossible to operate as written. Shipping under these numbers will immediately burn cash and collapse the service.
flaws.question: Which number is wrong: price, cost per video, or expected usage? Provide a corrected per-subscriber P&L showing margin at the declared price.

flaws.title: Compute cost estimate (≈2 per video) is asserted without a line-item or sensitivity
flaws.description: You claim ~2 per generated video but give no breakdown (inference GPU time, encoding, storage, retries, orchestration, CDN). Real costs vary by length, resolution, model, and load; spot/GPU price spikes will raise the true marginal cost. If the 2 figure is optimistic, the already-negative economics worsen rapidly.
flaws.question: Show a line-item cost breakdown and sensitivity (low/typical/high) for a 1‑minute, 3‑minute and 10‑minute video so we can verify the 2 per-video claim.

flaws.title: No evidence users will pay 5 for 'unlimited' or generate only 20 videos
flaws.description: You assume average usage of 20 videos/month at a 5 price point without market or behavioral evidence. If real users create more (or fewer) videos or reject the price, acquisition and retention metrics will change and economics will break. The product will be built to the wrong scale if this isn't tested first.

Incumbents can exploit this by offering a free bundled alternative and capturing the long tail.
flaws.question: What evidence (pipeline, lead volume, conversion funnel) shows demand is repeatable beyond these 24 studios?

execution_risk.summary: What breaks first: the referral/partnership acquisition engine — because there is no defined funnel, incentive structure, tracking or capacity to execute, so referrals will not convert or scale. Prevent it by: run an instrumented partner pilot (tracked referral codes, explicit partner incentive, partner onboarding flow) owned by a single partnerships lead before committing to scale. You have real traction (24 studios, £2,136 MRR) and 3 cancellations in six months; the plan extrapolates from these numbers directly into a channel that requires product hooks, contracts and Ops to work at scale, none of which are specified.

flaws.title: Referral/partnership channel is not a repeatable acquisition engine
flaws.description: The document says growth will come from referrals and partnerships with instructors but lists no funnel metrics, conversion targets, partner archetypes or pilot outcomes. Without a tested funnel (recruit → onboard → refer → close) you will get sporadic leads and no scalable pipeline; relying on goodwill from instructors will stall once initial contacts are exhausted. Building broad partnerships before proving conversion will burn time and misallocate scarce founder attention.
flaws.question: What exact funnel steps, conversion rates and pilot results prove an instructor partner will sign paying studios at scale?

flaws.title: No partner incentive or compensation model — instructors won't refer reliably
flaws.description: The plan assumes instructors will refer studios but does not state what, if anything, instructors get in return. Instructors will not act as a repeatable sales channel without a clear incentive (cash, credit, discount or product access) and a mechanism to capture and pay that incentive. Absent this, partnership outreach will produce conversations, not closed customers.
flaws.question: What specific incentive will you offer partners, who pays it, and how will you measure and attribute referral credit?

flaws.title: Retention/onboarding issues will swamp growth before scaling succeeds
flaws.description: You report 24 paying studios and 3 cancellations over six months but provide no churn rate, onboarding time, or cancellation reasons. If onboarding is manual or churn drivers unresolved, adding more signups via partners will just increase support load and churn, converting acquisition spend into churned revenue. Scaling partnerships without fixing onboarding and retention will make MRR growth illusionary.
flaws.question: What is your monthly churn rate, average onboarding time per studio, and the documented reasons for the 3 cancellations?

flaws.title: Payments and data compliance (PCI / GDPR) are unaddressed and will block scaling
flaws.description: You price in GBP and serve studios, which implies processing card payments and holding customer/pupil data subject to GDPR. There is no plan stating who handles payments, where data is hosted, or what contracts and controls exist. Scaling partnership and referrals increases data flows and liability; regulators or processors will stop onboarding unless controls are defined.
flaws.question: Who processes customer payments, where is customer data stored, and what PCI/GDPR controls and contracts do you currently have?

flaws.title: No partner onboarding, legal terms, or tracking infrastructure
flaws.description: Partnerships require signed agreements (referral terms), an onboarding playbook, referral tracking (codes or links), and a payments/commission plumbing. The plan lists 'partnerships' as a channel but omits these operational elements, so early partners will operate ad hoc, causing attribution disputes and poor experience. That operational gap will slow partner recruitment and make scaling chaotic.
flaws.question: What exact legal terms, onboarding materials and referral-tracking tools will you deploy to sign and operate partners?

flaws.title: Team and capacity to run partnerships and support studios is unspecified
flaws.description: No team, roles, or time allocation are listed. Running partnerships, onboarding studios, and providing support requires at least one dedicated partnerships/success owner; without it the founder becomes the bottleneck and execution grinds to a halt. The plan assumes scale without identifying who will execute day-to-day tasks.
flaws.question: Who will own partnerships, onboarding and support operations, and how many dedicated hires or hours will be allocated?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Mixed. Weakest number: '3 cancellations over six months' — because that figure is uninterpretable without starting customer counts or cohort churn, so LTV and retention cannot be calculated. Prove it by: provide a monthly cohort table (customers and MRR) for the last 12 months. Proven: current MRR and customer count reconcile (24 × £89 = £2,136).

flaws.title: No churn/retention metric — '3 cancellations' is uninterpretable
flaws.description: The document reports 3 cancellations over six months but gives no starting customer count, monthly active counts, or MRR by cohort. Without gross and net churn (monthly and annualized), you cannot compute customer lifetime or LTV, which is the single most important number for whether acquisition pays back. This gap makes any revenue or scaling claim unsupported because retention determines sustainable growth.
flaws.question: Provide the customer count at the start of the 6-month window, the date of each of the three cancellations, and a monthly cohort table (customers and MRR) for the last 12 months so gross/net churn and LTV can be calculated.

flaws.title: No CAC or acquisition performance data to justify referral/partnership scaling
flaws.description: You propose expanding via referrals and partnerships but give no acquisition spend, channel counts, or historical conversion rates. Without CAC (or number of customers won by referrals and their conversion rates) you cannot judge payback period or whether referrals alone can scale. Growth plans hinge on acquisition economics that are entirely absent.
flaws.question: Supply total acquisition spend (marketing + sales) and number of customers acquired in the last 6 and 12 months, and break out how many of the 24 came from referrals or partnerships so we can compute CAC and channel-specific conversion rates.

flaws.title: No measured evidence that referrals/partnerships convert at scale
flaws.description: The strategy names referrals and instructor partnerships as the growth channel but reports no referral conversion rate, average referrals per partner, or any partner commitments/pilot results. A claim that growth will come from this channel is an assumption until you show measured conversion and funnel volume. If referral conversion is low or partner reach is small, the stated channel will not deliver the required customers.
flaws.question: Show the measured referral funnel: referrals sent → trial/signups → paid for the last 6–12 months (n and %), and provide any partner pilot metrics or signed partner outreach commitments with expected referral volume.

flaws.title: Pricing validity at scale is not evidenced (£89 may not generalize)
flaws.description: Price and MRR reconcile for current customers (24 × 89 = 2136) but there is no evidence that this price will be accepted across the broader target market or across partner-referred leads. Pricing is load-bearing for LTV and acquisition payback; if price cannot be maintained at scale the economics collapse. You also provide no segmentation or willingness-to-pay checks.
flaws.question: Provide any price-sensitivity data: A/B price tests, survey or sales win rates at £89 versus other tiers, or churn split by customer segment that shows £89 is sustainable across your target studio population.

unit_economics.summary: Where the math breaks: CAC and cost-to-serve — because you have a price (£89/mo) and 24 customers (MRR £2,136) but no measured CAC, no per-customer operating costs, and no LTV or payback calculation to show acquisition pays back. Prove otherwise by: reporting measured CAC by channel (referral, partnership), per-customer variable costs (hosting, payments, support) and a resulting LTV:CAC or payback period. Currently the numbers stated (24 studios, £2,136 MRR, 3 cancellations in six months) are real but insufficient — without CAC and unit costs you cannot know if scaling by the proposed channels is financially viable.

flaws.title: No measured CAC despite relying entirely on referrals/partnerships
flaws.description: You state growth will come from referrals and partnerships but also explicitly say you haven't measured how well either works. CAC is the single place where growth assumptions meet finance; without a measured CAC by channel you cannot show payback or LTV:CAC. This is fatal to any revenue projection that assumes scaling.
flaws.question: What is the measured CAC (including all channel costs, incentives and onboarding) for referrals and for partnership-sourced customers?

flaws.title: No cost-to-serve (unit cost) provided — compute, storage, support, payments missing
flaws.description: The document gives price and MRR but no breakdown of per-customer variable costs: hosting, storage, API/third-party fees, payment processing fees, and support time. You cannot compute gross margin or per-customer contribution without these. At SaaS price points, variable costs and required support can make or break unit economics.
flaws.question: Provide a per-customer monthly variable cost breakdown (hosting/compute, storage, payment fees, support FTE minutes and cost, third-party integrations) and the resulting gross margin per customer.

flaws.title: Willingness-to-pay and pricing validation not documented
flaws.description: Price is set at £89/mo with 24 paying studios but there is no evidence this price is market-validated or that segments will convert at scale at £89. Current customers could be early adopters willing to pay more than the broader market. If widespread conversion at £89 fails, the whole CAC math and payback falls apart.
flaws.question: Show pricing validation: cohort conversion rates, any price testing, or willingness-to-pay evidence across a representative sample of target studios.

flaws.title: LTV, churn, and payback period not calculated despite churn signal
flaws.description: You reported 3 cancellations in six months but did not provide cohort churn rate, average lifetime, or LTV. Without LTV you cannot compare to CAC or compute payback. The single churn datapoint is insufficient to determine if CAC will ever pay back within an acceptable timeframe.
flaws.question: Provide monthly churn rate (by cohort if possible), average customer lifetime, resulting LTV (using your gross margin), and the payback period on CAC.

flaws.title: Gross margin at scale is undefined — unknown fixed vs variable cost allocation
flaws.description: There is no projection of how gross margin changes as you scale. Fixed costs (platform, support headcount, compliance) and variable costs (payment fees, hosting) must be separated to model margin at 100s–1000s of studios. Without this you cannot predict unit economics at scale or when break-even on operating expenses occurs.
flaws.question: Provide fixed and variable cost assumptions and a model showing gross margin at current scale and at target scale (e.g., 500 studios).

flaws.title: Hidden operational costs (refunds, chargebacks, fraud, compliance, moderation) are unaccounted
flaws.description: No line items or risk allowances are shown for refunds, chargebacks, fraud, tax/compliance, or content moderation. These can be meaningful for payments-based B2B products and will reduce effective revenue and increase support burden. They are often nonlinear as you scale or enter new regions.
flaws.question: Estimate expected refund/chargeback rates, fraud loss, and any compliance or payment-onboarding costs per customer (or state why they are immaterial).

execution_risk.summary: What breaks first: channel–buyer mismatch — because the plan relies on fitness instructors to drive signups for a product sold and billed to independent studios, and the document contains no evidence instructors can or will close studio purchases. Prevent it by: running a tight pilot that requires instructors to deliver warm intros that convert into signed studio contracts (or at least meetings with decision-makers) before you invest in partner programs. The rest of the plan extrapolates growth from that single, unmeasured channel, while ignoring retention, partner operations, and compliance needs that will block scaling once acquisition starts.

flaws.title: Channel–buyer mismatch: instructors aren't the paying decision-makers
flaws.description: You plan to expand through partnerships with fitness instructors while explicitly selling to independent fitness studios. Instructors typically lack procurement authority and budget control at studios; relying on them shifts the burden to introduce and close studio owners without demonstrating that instructors can influence purchase decisions. If instructors cannot reliably generate qualified, studio-level signups the growth channel collapses before CAC or product-market fit can be meaningfully measured.
flaws.question: Can you produce documented examples where an instructor referral directly resulted in a signed studio subscription (not just an intro), and who at the studio signed and paid?

flaws.title: Acquisition channels are untested and assumed scalable
flaws.description: You state growth will come from referrals and instructor partnerships but explicitly note these haven't been measured. Scaling requires measured CAC, funnel conversion rates, and predictable lead velocity; none are provided. Without those metrics you will either burn cash on ineffective channels or under-invest in the right channel and stall growth.
flaws.question: What is the measured conversion rate and CAC from any referral or instructor partnership you've run so far?

flaws.title: No partner ops, tracking, or payout flows — partnerships will stall in execution
flaws.description: Turning instructors into a channel requires partner onboarding, tracking links, attribution, contract templates, and commission or incentive payouts. The document contains no sequencing or product work to support partner-facing flows, so onboarding will become manual, error-prone and non-scalable the moment you recruit more than a few partners. Manual partner handling will consume founder time and kill velocity.
flaws.question: What partner onboarding, attribution, legal, and payout processes will you ship in the next 90 days to make instructor partnerships repeatable?

flaws.title: Retention/churn hidden by a single cancellation stat
flaws.description: You report 3 cancellations over six months but provide no cohort churn rate, monthly churn, or LTV estimate. Sequencing is backwards: you plan to scale acquisition before proving studios retain the product. If churn is materially above a sustainable rate, any scaled acquisition will be wasted and MRR will not compound.
flaws.question: What is your monthly and cohort churn rate and the current LTV:CAC based on the 24 paying studios and the 3 cancellations?

flaws.title: Compliance, payments and data-handling are unaddressed
flaws.description: At scale you'll need clear answers for payments processing, VAT/tax on SaaS for studios, and data protection (client health data, GDPR) — plus contracts for partner payouts. None of these operational and regulatory items are mentioned, so legal or payment blockers will appear as you expand across regions or add partner commissions. These blockers will delay launches in new territories and complicate customer onboarding.
flaws.question: How will you handle payments, tax (VAT), data protection (GDPR), and partner commission contracts as you onboard more studios and partners?
